exactBefore.body:
## Chef's Note

Homemade wonton wrappers have a delicate, silky texture that's hard to match with store-bought. The dough should be quite firm after kneading, then rested for 30-60 minutes to relax the gluten so you can roll it paper-thin. The key: use cornstarch for dusting between sheets, never flour. Flour will absorb into the dough and make it gummy, while cornstarch keeps them separate and provides a smooth finish when boiled.

## Directions

1.  **Mix:** In a large bowl, whisk the flour and salt. Make a well in the center. Add the egg and water. Mix until a shaggy dough forms.
2.  **Knead:** Turn out onto a clean surface and knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should be quite firm.
3.  **Rest:** Wrap in plastic and let rest at room temperature for at least 30-60 minutes. This relaxes the gluten so you can roll it paper-thin.
4.  **Roll:** Divide dough into 4 pieces. Use a pasta machine (recommended) or a heavy rolling pin. Roll until the dough is thin enough to see your hand through it (Setting 6 or 7 on most pasta machines).
5.  **Cut:** Dust generously with cornstarch. Cut into 3.5-inch squares.
6.  **Store:** Stack with plenty of cornstarch between layers. Wrap tightly in plastic. (Can be refrigerated for 2 days or frozen for 3 months).

steps.title: Mix
steps.text: Combine {{ingredients}} in a bowl: first whisk the flour and salt, then make a well and mix in the beaten egg and water. Stir and press until a firm, shaggy dough forms. Do not taste the raw dough.

steps.title: Knead
steps.text: Knead for about 10 minutes until the dough holds together and becomes more elastic. If persistent dry crumbs will not join the dough, work in {{ingredients}}, stopping as soon as they adhere. The dough should be firm rather than sticky or soft.

steps.title: Rest covered
steps.text: Wrap tightly and rest for 30–60 minutes so the dough becomes easier to roll. In a kitchen above 90°F, rest in the refrigerator instead. Keep track of total counter time from mixing onward, including rolling; refrigerate the dough if work is interrupted.

steps.title: Roll thin sheets
steps.text: Divide the dough into manageable pieces, about four for the original batch, and keep the pieces you are not rolling covered; refrigerate them if rolling is slow. Larger batches may need more pieces rather than larger sheets. Flatten one piece into a rectangle and dust both sides with {{ingredients}}. With a pasta roller, start at its widest opening and pass the dough through progressively narrower openings, keeping the sheet even. Cut a long sheet crosswise if it becomes awkward to handle. With a rolling pin, roll evenly from the center outward, giving dough that springs back another brief covered rest. Stop just short of paper thin: the sheet should be evenly thin and flexible, but still lift and fold without tearing. Machine numbers vary, so use the sheet itself as the guide. Re-dust sheets and finished wrappers with the same cornstarch as needed to keep them separate.

steps.title: Cut and cover
steps.text: Cut into approximately 3½-inch squares with a knife or pizza cutter and a straightedge. Keep cut wrappers covered as you work so the edges stay pliable. Gather clean offcuts, press them together, cover and rest briefly before rolling them again. For the original batch, expect about 60 wrappers, but thickness, trimming and re-rolling change the count.

steps.title: Fill or chill promptly
steps.text: Fill the wrappers as they are made, using a wonton filling recipe and cooking the filled wontons according to that recipe. Keep the uncooked filling chilled while working. For a pause, stack the dusted wrappers in small portions, cover tightly and refrigerate promptly at 40°F or below. Plan to use cut wrappers the same day. Count mixing, resting, rolling and filling together: keep total time out of refrigeration under 2 hours, or under 1 hour above 90°F.

steps.title: Freeze unused wrappers
steps.text: For longer storage, promptly pack dusted wrappers in flat portions separated with parchment, wrap airtight and freeze at 0°F. Thaw a wrapped portion in the refrigerator and use the same day. The dough and wrappers still need thorough cooking; freezing does not make raw flour or egg ready to eat.

learning.focus: Control dough firmness, sheet thickness and chilled holding.
learning.outcome: Evenly thin, flexible squares with pliable edges for filled wontons.
before: Have the filling recipe ready and keep its uncooked filling chilled.
The measured water is a starting amount; egg size, flour and humidity can change whether a few extra drops are needed.
For the original batch, expect roughly 60 wrappers cut into 3½-inch squares; thickness and trimming change the count.
This wheat-and-egg dough suits the linked pork-and-shrimp wontons. Har gow is a distinct starch-dough recipe; this dough does not replace its wrapper.

checkpoints.cue: The dough coheres but remains firm, with no pool of moisture or persistent loose crumbs.
checkpoints.why: Too much water makes very thin sheets difficult to handle, while dry fragments tear during rolling.

checkpoints.cue: The sheet is just short of paper thin, even across its width and flexible enough to lift without tearing.
checkpoints.why: Physical thickness and handling transfer between machines; a numbered setting does not.

checkpoints.cue: The edges stay covered and pliable, and raw dough and filling are chilled during pauses.
checkpoints.why: Dry edges resist sealing, while the egg dough and filling need controlled counter time.

troubleshooting.problem: The sheet springs back while rolling.
troubleshooting.cause: The dough needs more time to relax.
troubleshooting.fix: Cover it for a brief rest, chilling if the counter-time limit is near, and then continue rolling gradually.

troubleshooting.cause: There is too little cornstarch between the surfaces, or the dough is too wet.
troubleshooting.fix: Dust both sides lightly but thoroughly, cover the stack, and keep the next sheets firm rather than adding uncontrolled water.

troubleshooting.problem: Thin sheets tear or cut edges crack.
troubleshooting.cause: The sheet is uneven, excessively thin or drying uncovered.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop one increment thicker, keep unworked dough and wrappers covered, and re-rest gathered offcuts before rolling.

learning.storage: Use freshly cut wrappers the same day, keeping covered at 40°F or below during pauses. The tightly wrapped whole egg dough may be refrigerated through overnight, then rolled the next day; allow only the working piece to become pliable while keeping the rest chilled. For longer holding, promptly freeze dusted wrappers in airtight flat portions at 0°F and thaw them wrapped in the refrigerator for same-day use. Keep total time out of refrigeration below 2 hours, or below 1 hour above 90°F, counting mixing, rest and rolling. Wash hands and work surfaces after raw flour and egg; do not taste the dough, and cook filled wontons thoroughly according to the filling recipe.
learning.timing: Allow about 45–75 minutes of active mixing, kneading, rolling and cutting, plus the 30–60-minute covered rest. Plan on about 75–135 minutes; hand rolling and chilling pauses can take longer. Refrigerate dough waiting its turn so a long project does not mean uninterrupted counter holding. Filling and cooking time belongs to the filled-wonton recipe. Scaled batches need additional work periods and chilled holding; roller numbers and times do not scale.

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

A firm dough and a covered rest make thin sheets easier to handle. Cornstarch helps keep the sheets and cut wrappers separate. Roll by the feel and evenness of the sheet rather than a machine number, and cover each small batch so the edges remain pliable for folding.

## Directions

1. **Mix:** Combine all-purpose flour, kosher salt, egg, and water in a bowl: first whisk the flour and salt, then make a well and mix in the beaten egg and water. Stir and press until a firm, shaggy dough forms. Do not taste the raw dough.
2. **Knead:** Knead for about 10 minutes until the dough holds together and becomes more elastic. If persistent dry crumbs will not join the dough, work in additional water, stopping as soon as they adhere. The dough should be firm rather than sticky or soft.
3. **Rest covered:** Wrap tightly and rest for 30–60 minutes so the dough becomes easier to roll. In a kitchen above 90°F, rest in the refrigerator instead. Keep track of total counter time from mixing onward, including rolling; refrigerate the dough if work is interrupted.
4. **Roll thin sheets:** Divide the dough into manageable pieces, about four for the original batch, and keep the pieces you are not rolling covered; refrigerate them if rolling is slow. Larger batches may need more pieces rather than larger sheets. Flatten one piece into a rectangle and dust both sides with cornstarch. With a pasta roller, start at its widest opening and pass the dough through progressively narrower openings, keeping the sheet even. Cut a long sheet crosswise if it becomes awkward to handle. With a rolling pin, roll evenly from the center outward, giving dough that springs back another brief covered rest. Stop just short of paper thin: the sheet should be evenly thin and flexible, but still lift and fold without tearing. Machine numbers vary, so use the sheet itself as the guide. Re-dust sheets and finished wrappers with the same cornstarch as needed to keep them separate.
5. **Cut and cover:** Cut into approximately 3½-inch squares with a knife or pizza cutter and a straightedge. Keep cut wrappers covered as you work so the edges stay pliable. Gather clean offcuts, press them together, cover and rest briefly before rolling them again. For the original batch, expect about 60 wrappers, but thickness, trimming and re-rolling change the count.
6. **Fill or chill promptly:** Fill the wrappers as they are made, using a wonton filling recipe and cooking the filled wontons according to that recipe. Keep the uncooked filling chilled while working. For a pause, stack the dusted wrappers in small portions, cover tightly and refrigerate promptly at 40°F or below. Plan to use cut wrappers the same day. Count mixing, resting, rolling and filling together: keep total time out of refrigeration under 2 hours, or under 1 hour above 90°F.
7. **Freeze unused wrappers:** For longer storage, promptly pack dusted wrappers in flat portions separated with parchment, wrap airtight and freeze at 0°F. Thaw a wrapped portion in the refrigerator and use the same day. The dough and wrappers still need thorough cooking; freezing does not make raw flour or egg ready to eat.
